title: The Honest Venom
text:
Shan unrolls the cloth in the lamp's small pool of light. She holds it close, she holds it far; she does neither of these things as long as she holds it still, at the lamp's exact distance, while her breath slows.

'Moon-Silt,' she says, finally. 'A pill only three apothecaries alive can brew. One died last winter; one has gone west. The third lives at the mouth of the Pavilion — I will not name her; the valley's quiet is her quiet too. She does not brew for strangers. Someone she owes a debt to has called the debt.'

She lays the cloth aside, without ceremony.

'I will not tell you who. I will tell you: the merchant lives. Carry this pearl to his wife. The counter-venom is simple; the knowing is the hard part. And when the Pavilion next asks whether the valley can be bought, tell them the valley already knows what they have, and at what price, and who brewed it.'

She does not smile.

'That is the Pavilion's payment for the poison. It has been paid. There will be no other.'

title: The Sword That Would Not Strike
text:
The Azure Cloud disciple is eighteen. Her name is Yanyu. She was sent south with a letter she did not read, to a disciple she was told to assess. Her sword never left its sheath.

On the return road she drew it to clean it — a courtesy to the blade — and the blade refused her grip, because a poison had been worked into the hilt-wrap a week before by a junior brother whose senior brother she had embarrassed at the third bell.

She stumbled into the Thousand Venom Valley because the Valley was on her route and because her legs had begun to do what legs do when the body wants to deliver itself to someone who will not let it rot.

Shan's gatekeeper caught her in the fog at the steles. Shan drew the poison in an hour and a half, and then she sat beside the girl until morning without speaking, because the valley does not lecture the cranes about what the cranes owe their own.

The letter the girl had been carrying was never read. Shan placed it, unopened, back inside the girl's sash before the disciples of the Cloud came to collect her.

'Let them find it,' she said afterwards. 'Let them find what someone decided was less important than this child. Let them read it in their own hall, and not in mine.'

title: The Hand That Empties the Heart
text:
Lan-yi walked the earth curing plagues for seven years. In the eighth she sat with a dying serpent she had raised by hand, and the serpent would not drink the water she offered.

'There are hands,' she wrote afterwards in the margin of her first treatise, 'that are honest enough to fill. There are hands honest enough to empty. The valley asks of its Matriarch the second kind. It is not the harder of the two.

It is only the one everyone pretends does not exist.'

This is the passage Shan reads on the morning a basin-creature will not drink. She reads it once, closes the book, and does not read again.

The hand that empties the heart has a single small rite. The Matriarch takes the hundred-grass in two fingers; she offers it to the creature from the palm of the other hand; if the creature will not take it, she waits. She does not force the grass; she does not withdraw it. She waits until the creature sleeps without drinking. She sits with the sleep. That is the whole of the rite.

The rite is not for witness. The Matriarch is alone in the hall when the basin is emptied, and the next viper — chosen that same day from the gorge — knows, when it enters the bronze, that the last sister was not hurried.

title: The Hundred-Grass
text:
The hundred-grass (*bai-cao* in the old tongue) does not grow where other plants have lived, or where other plants are growing, or where any other plant has ever tried and failed.

It grows where no plant has *ever attempted*. The distinction matters.

A square of earth where wheat failed is no good. A square where no wheat was ever planted but weeds have ventured — no good. A square where the wind carried a seed once, and the seed lay dormant for a season and rotted — no good.

The hundred-grass needs the absence of even the trying. It grows in the garden's iron-lattice corners where the wind's geometry makes seed-landing itself impossible, and it grows nowhere else in the world.

In the Poisoner's Garden, at midnight, if you walk the corners slowly enough, you will see it: a pale blade so thin it is almost a thought. Pick one. Pick only one.

It is the valley's oldest medicine. It is the only antidote the serpent accepts. It is the only antidote the serpent has ever been asked to accept.

Lan-yi wrote, at the end of the treatise: 'If the garden does not grow it for you tonight, do not return tomorrow. The garden has decided tonight is your answer. Both answers are also answers.'
